consumer_seed: The Ofcom digital-landline guide was published on 13 December 2021.
The Ofcom digital-landline guide was last updated on 16 September 2024.
Traditional landline calls have been delivered over the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN).
Ofcom states that BT decided to retire the PSTN by January 2027.
Future landline calls will be delivered using Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP), which uses a broadband connection.
Ofcom says PSTN equipment was developed and installed in the UK in the 1980s.
The old PSTN equipment is becoming harder and more expensive to maintain.
A landline provider should contact its customer when migration to a new telephone service applies.
Customers do not need to act until their provider says the telephone service is changing or they choose to change it.
After migration to VoIP, the phone will generally plug into a broadband router rather than the wall phone socket.
A provider should arrange any required new router or broadband installation for the migrated landline service.
Some fire alarms, burglar alarms and telecare devices that rely on a phone line may need replacement or reconfiguration.
Customers who retain a landline after PSTN switch-off will generally need a suitable connection even if they do not use broadband services.
Ofcom expects options that do not force landline-only customers to buy a high-speed broadband package.
A VoIP phone connected through a mains-powered broadband router will not work in a power cut without additional support.
Providers must enable landline-reliant customers to contact emergency services during a power cut, for example through battery backup or a basic mobile phone.
The Ofcom BT landline-only page was published on 10 December 2020.
The Ofcom BT landline-only page was last updated on 16 March 2026.
BT confirmed a £1 per month line-rental increase for landline-only customers from 31 March 2026.
BT confirmed no increase in call-plan charges for this landline-only group.
The stated landline-only pricing arrangement applies for 12 months from 31 March 2026.
BT landline-only customers have a BT landline but no broadband with BT or another provider.
Ofcom says the BT landline-only customer group is shrinking over time.
Ofcom says the group is largely older and switches provider less often than younger customer groups.
Ofcom intends to monitor BT's landline-only pricing through its regular consumer-price monitoring.
BT offers an eligible-customer landline-only social tariff priced at £10 per month.
The Ofcom provider-closure guide was published on 13 February 2026.
When another company takes over a failed broadband or landline provider, customers can continue using the services they had.
Ofcom says a takeover should in most cases occur without interruption to service.
An existing contract should in most cases transfer to the new provider.
If the acquiring provider changes contract terms, customers should have a right to leave without an early termination charge.
A customer unhappy with the acquiring provider can switch to another provider.
Before switching, customers should check whether they are still within a minimum contract period.
If no company takes over, the broadband or landline service will stop on a specified date.
The failed provider should tell customers when service will stop.
A customer must sign up with a new provider to continue service when no takeover occurs.
Customers should not have to pay early termination charges when switching after a provider closes without a takeover.
It might not be possible to keep the existing phone number after a provider closes without a takeover.
The Ofcom scam-protection guide was published on 15 July 2026.
The Ofcom scam-protection guide was last updated on 22 July 2026.
For suspicious contact, Ofcom advises not replying, clicking links, pressing buttons or sharing personal details.
Ofcom advises checking for urgency, unexpected requests or suspicious links before acting.
Suspicious text messages can be forwarded to 7726.
People should not give unexpected callers personal details such as bank information, PINs or passwords.
Ofcom advises hanging up when there is doubt about a caller's identity.
Ofcom advises not allowing a caller to rush a decision.
An organisation should be called back using a number from its official website or another published source, not a number supplied by the caller.
A caller knowing personal details does not prove that the caller is genuine.
Ofcom advises not clicking links in unexpected texts even when they appear to come from a recognised sender.
Replying to an unknown text can confirm that the phone number is active.
Forwarding suspicious texts to 7726 is free of charge.
For payment or login requests, Ofcom advises going directly to the organisation's website rather than using a supplied link.
A suspicious call or message should be ended or ignored before contacting the organisation directly.
Ofcom suggests searching a phone number or sender name because other people may have reported scam numbers.
A callback number supplied by a caller should be checked independently before use.
Investment offers can be checked against the Financial Conduct Authority register before action is taken.
Ofcom recommends talking to a trusted person before acting on suspicious contact.
Most smartphones allow specific numbers to be blocked from call logs or messages.
Many phones include built-in spam filters for calls and texts.
Some providers offer network-level filtering that blocks known scam numbers before they reach customers.
Scammers can fake the number displayed by caller ID, a practice known as number spoofing.
